evianchezvous.seoTitle: Evianchezvous — React + Magento 2 e-commerce · Emeric Guyon
evianchezvous.description: Headless rebuild of evianchezvous: Magento 1 to 2, React + GraphQL front-end.
evianchezvous.longDescription: Full rebuild of evianchezvous, Evian's home water delivery site (Paris / Île-de-France): migration from a monolithic Magento 1 to headless Magento 2, with a React + GraphQL front-end. I was front-end tech lead for 2 years, from scoping through to production.
evianchezvous.approach: The project meant doing everything at once: migrating Magento 1 to 2, pulling the front out of the monolith into a React app, rethinking checkout and the customer account, and porting the subscription logic (recurring water delivery) that Magento doesn't ship with out of the box. SSR ran underneath to protect search rankings, and performance had to beat the V1 from day one.
evianchezvous.takeaway1: React front-end built from scratch across the full e-commerce tunnel: cart, checkout, account, subscriptions, postal-code-based delivery slots. All the business logic moved over to JS.
evianchezvous.takeaway2: Custom GraphQL layer on top of Magento 2: native M2 doesn't cover everything, so I wrote plenty of custom resolvers and extended schemas to serve the front without unnecessary round-trips.
evianchezvous.takeaway3: Subscription module, recurring payments and one-shot orders, wired into per-zone delivery constraints. Magento can't handle that alone, so I coded it custom on both sides.
evianchezvous.stackNote: Magento 2 on the back for the e-commerce stack (catalog, orders, customers, payments), with a custom-extended GraphQL layer. React + Apollo Client + SSR on the front for performance and SEO: pulling out of a Magento monolith without losing indexation is the whole headless bet. React also enables a real mobile experience, with components designed for touch and native-feeling transitions, that Magento 1 simply couldn't deliver. Then the M1 to M2 data migration itself (products, customers, orders, active subscriptions) without breaking history.
evianchezvous.result: Still live years after delivery, with performance and conversion rate up compared to the Magento 1 version. On a personal level, this was my first React e-commerce site and my first front-end tech lead role over 2 years. The main lesson: moving Magento to headless means rebuilding in React things the old version gave you for free, like cart, sessions, customer flows. A lot of plumbing to lay back down just to gain on UX and performance.
evianchezvous.seoDescription: Headless rebuild of the Evianchezvous e-commerce site: Magento 1 to 2 migration, React + GraphQL front-end. Delivered by Emeric Guyon, freelance developer.

ekkinox.seoTitle: Ekkinox — construction finance tool in Vue.js · Emeric Guyon
ekkinox.description: Construction-site financial tracking tool, built in-house at Patriarche, then turned into a white-label product.
ekkinox.longDescription: Custom business tool for construction-site financial tracking, started as an internal Patriarche product then turned into a white-label version with a SaaS path ahead. I was senior front-end and front lead for 18 months, on a team of 2 front, 2 back, 1 PM and 1 designer.
ekkinox.approach: We started out wanting a modular setup, but the domain turned out too interconnected for that, so we went with a domain-oriented organization structured around interfaces. That split follows the UX designer's mental model and how people actually use the tool. We ran business workshops for every feature, iterated fast, and did regular client demos. We adjusted often, sometimes heavily, without ever losing the overall coherence.
ekkinox.takeaway1: Domain-oriented front-end architecture built to last 18 months of delivery, split by interfaces aligned with UX flows rather than by file type. No components/utils/views folder ballooning out of control.
ekkinox.takeaway2: Tailor-made business views: financial tables, custom behavior per module, and an in-house design system built alongside the product to stay coherent as features piled up.
ekkinox.takeaway3: Recurring user workshops and client demos at every milestone. Learning construction-site finance on the job became part of the role, not a side concern.
ekkinox.stackNote: Vue + TypeScript and Pinia on the front, with an in-house design system built in parallel with the product. NestJS on the back, full TypeScript end to end. Front-end architecture was the structuring topic: a strict domain split wouldn't have held since everything is linked, so we went for an interface-based split that maps to the business and how people actually use it.
ekkinox.result: 18 months on the project, from day one through the move to a white-label version, with a front-end architecture that never had to be rewritten along the way. On a personal level, this was my first real front-lead role over the long haul: a chance to lay foundations that hold, push back on the PM when it mattered, and learn a domain (construction-site finance) deep enough to talk to users without hand-waving.
ekkinox.seoDescription: Ekkinox, a construction-site financial tracking tool built in Vue.js and TypeScript for Patriarche (Chambéry, France), later shipped as a white-label product.

25lieuxinnovation.seoTitle: 25 Lieux Innovation — WordPress + GSAP site · Emeric Guyon
25lieuxinnovation.description: Editorial site built around the 25 places transforming innovation in France.
25lieuxinnovation.longDescription: Editorial site spotlighting 25 places that are transforming innovation in France, an in-house Patriarche project built around a book, site and event trio. Full-custom WordPress with custom post types and taxonomies, Timber for Twig templating, ACF Pro for editorial blocks, and a fair amount of GSAP work to bring the content to life as you scroll.
25lieuxinnovation.approach: An editorial site with rich source material (long-form text, photos, places sorted by category), where the front-end challenge was avoiding a flat reading experience. I went with scroll storytelling: crafted reveals, transitions between places, and a layout that lets photo and text breathe in alternation. On the CMS side, I left default WordPress behind and gave editors a back-office aligned with how they actually think.
25lieuxinnovation.takeaway1: GSAP / ScrollTrigger scroll storytelling: scroll-driven reveals, parallax, pinning, transitions between places. Motion in service of the editorial, not decoration for its own sake.
25lieuxinnovation.takeaway2: Full-custom WordPress: custom post types for the places, dedicated taxonomies for category filtering, ACF Pro for modular editorial blocks on the admin side.
25lieuxinnovation.takeaway3: Timber + Twig to separate logic from view, so the codebase stays maintainable instead of turning into the single.php soup that gets unreadable fast as a project grows.
25lieuxinnovation.stackNote: WordPress with Timber + ACF Pro, my go-to setup for full-custom WordPress done cleanly. Timber gives real logic/view separation (Twig on the template side), and ACF Pro turns the admin into a place editors can actually work in. GSAP + ScrollTrigger handle the motion layer on the front, the right tools for an editorial site that needs room to breathe.
25lieuxinnovation.result: Site is live. On a personal level, this is the project where I really pushed GSAP further, past simple fades and into real motion writing that serves the editorial content.
25lieuxinnovation.seoDescription: Fully custom WordPress editorial site with GSAP animations for 25 Lieux Innovation. Designed and developed by Emeric Guyon, freelance developer in Chambéry.

lonn.seoTitle: Lonn — wellness scheduling SaaS in Symfony · Emeric Guyon
lonn.description: B2B SaaS for wellness centers: staff scheduling and appointment booking.
lonn.longDescription: B2B SaaS for wellness centers: a staff scheduling module on the manager side (pre-payroll-style, working-time rules) and an appointment booking system on the client side. The MVP was built as a team via Le Collectif 40, and I was responsible for the backend architecture, the data model and the server-side technical choices.
lonn.approach: My job on the server side: lay an architecture that holds, model a clean database that lets two scopes coexist (HR scheduling and client bookings) without them bleeding into each other, and expose it all through a custom Symfony BFF API. I stayed in continuous dialogue with the client, who acted as product owner, and every scope trade-off and every business rule got discussed before it was settled. I kept strict MVP discipline: cut what doesn't fit V1 rather than ship late.
lonn.takeaway1: Backend architecture and data model designed to let two scopes coexist (staff scheduling and client bookings) without stepping on each other.
lonn.takeaway2: A Symfony BFF API designed for a single client (the Vue front-end): aggregation, clear contracts, business-rule validation centralized server-side.
lonn.takeaway3: MVP scope held: cut feature by feature to lay clean foundations, ready to be extended.
lonn.stackNote: Symfony was requested by the client, a solid framework for carrying business logic. PostgreSQL for persistence: a mature ORM and relational guarantees that pay off the moment HR data and calendar data start mixing. On the front, Vue + TypeScript, built by another team member, gave us a stable, typed API contract and a front that doesn't duplicate the logic.
lonn.result: MVP shipped. Nothing louder than that: the goal was to lay the foundations cleanly and hold the scope. For me, this was the project where the discipline of what does NOT belong in V1 sat at the heart of the brief, and where the architecture I set early on directly determined how fast we could deliver.
lonn.seoDescription: Lonn, a B2B scheduling and appointment-booking SaaS for wellness centers, built with Symfony and Vue.js. Architecture, front-end and API integration.

elitetrackr.seoTitle: EliteTrackr — athletics data platform · Emeric Guyon
elitetrackr.description: My take on the Wikipedia of athletics. 800K athletes, 14M performances, 230 countries, 9 languages.
elitetrackr.role: Solo · Design, dev, devops, data, SEO
elitetrackr.longDescription: I did track and field for years. Every time I wanted to dig into a performance, compare a season, or follow an athlete's trajectory, I'd end up on sites capped at the Olympics or the biggest meets, never the full picture, never the tools to actually tell a story with the numbers. So I built it myself. EliteTrackr aims to become the Wikipedia of athletics: a global, multilingual reference where raw data turns readable again, for fans, athletes, coaches.
elitetrackr.approach: Shipping this alone meant solving three separate problems: get the data in, make it indexable everywhere, and keep it protected. Each one came with its own constraints, from a pipeline that has to digest 14 million performances to infrastructure that holds up against scrapers and AI bots.
elitetrackr.takeaway1: A Python pipeline that pulls data from several sources and consolidates it into one database: 800,000 athletes, 14 million performances, 230 countries, and it grows a bit more every day.
elitetrackr.takeaway2: Nuxt SSR + i18n across 9 languages, with an indexing strategy tuned per market. No ads, no growth hacking, the data quality does the rest.
elitetrackr.takeaway3: Cloudflare sits in front to absorb bots, AI scrapers and attacks. Redis caches the hot queries. I built the architecture defensively from day one.
elitetrackr.stackNote: Full-JS to share types end to end between Nuxt and AdonisJS, and to ship Adonis in production, a deliberate bet on my part. Python handles the data layer: better raw performance and a data-science ecosystem nothing else matches. Postgres for persistence, Redis for cache, Coolify for deployment.
elitetrackr.result: Live since January 2026. About 50 visitors a day, pure organic growth, no paid acquisition. Lighthouse scores of 99/92/96 on desktop and 80/92/96 on mobile, on pages serving up to 14 million records. I did all of it solo: design, UI/UX, front, back, devops, data, SEO. Beyond the numbers, this is the project where I found my voice, visual, tone, structure, and where I get to watch the database grow a little richer every day.
elitetrackr.seoDescription: EliteTrackr, an athletics data platform: 800K athletes, 14M performances, 230 countries, 9 languages. Nuxt, AdonisJS, Python, D3. Solo project by Emeric Guyon.

juriscan.seoTitle: Juriscan — AI legal data extraction · Emeric Guyon
juriscan.description: MVP for AI-powered data extraction from legal documents, a fully local OCR plus LLM pipeline.
juriscan.longDescription: MVP for automated data extraction from legal documents (writs of summons, enforcement orders, official reports) for a firm of judicial officers. OCR plus AI interpretation, structured field extraction, export into the client's internal CRM. One month, solo, as a freelancer, from scoping to delivery.
juriscan.approach: The core of it is a two-stage pipeline. First an OCR with layout understanding runs on the PDF, then an LLM reads the resulting markdown and identifies the fields to extract (parties, dates, amounts, addresses) per document type. Everything runs locally on GPU, no cloud APIs: the data is sensitive and the client wouldn't have it any other way. A Rust worker orchestrates multithreading and keeps throughput acceptable on batches of PDFs.
juriscan.takeaway1: Fully self-hosted AI pipeline: DeepSeek-OCR for the read, DeepSeek-Coder-V2 for structuring, llama.cpp + CUDA for inference. Data never leaves the client's server.
juriscan.takeaway2: Rust worker for multithreading and orchestration: parallel OCR, predictable memory. Node would have folded under this kind of volume.
juriscan.takeaway3: Vue 3 + shadcn-vue front: upload, PDF preview on the left, editable extracted data on the right, CSV export to the client CRM.
juriscan.stackNote: AdonisJS 6 + PostgreSQL for persistence and the API on the back. Vue 3 + Tailwind + shadcn-vue on the front. The centerpiece is the infrastructure: a Rust worker that calls DeepSeek-OCR then DeepSeek-Coder-V2 (via llama.cpp) on a local GPU, multithreaded, deployed via Docker + NVIDIA Container Toolkit. Everything stays self-hosted: a firm of judicial officers can't exactly send its documents to OpenAI.
juriscan.result: MVP delivered, currently in testing on the client side. On a personal level, this was my first real AI project, and the first one I built mostly paired with an AI coding assistant. A stack I didn't know going in (Rust, llama.cpp, local DeepSeek on CUDA), learned and shipped in one month. It's exactly the kind of case where an assistant speeds you up without degrading quality, as long as you stay in charge of the architecture.
juriscan.seoDescription: Juriscan, an MVP for AI-powered extraction of legal data: fully local OCR + LLM pipeline in AdonisJS, DeepSeek and Rust. Document confidentiality guaranteed.

parentsdouceur.seoTitle: ParentsDouceur — WordPress showcase site · Emeric Guyon
parentsdouceur.description: Custom WordPress vitrine site for an independent perinatal practitioner. Solo UI/UX + dev.
parentsdouceur.longDescription: Vitrine site for an independent perinatal and parental practitioner. I handled UI/UX and development, working directly with the practitioner. Full-custom WordPress (ACF + Timber), GSAP for soft animations.
parentsdouceur.approach: A small solo project in direct contact with the client: a practitioner who wanted a site that felt like her, warm, soft, feminine. I went with a maternal art direction (pastels, curves, serif type) and kept the motion restrained, just enough for the page to breathe.
parentsdouceur.takeaway1: Soft, maternal art direction: pastel palette, curved shapes, warm serif typography.
parentsdouceur.takeaway2: Full-custom WordPress with Timber + ACF Pro, a clean back-office so the practitioner can update content on her own.
parentsdouceur.takeaway3: Discreet GSAP animations serving the mood, not stealing the show.
parentsdouceur.stackNote: WordPress with Timber + ACF Pro for a back-office a non-technical person can actually use, GSAP for the motion layer. A stack matched to the scope: a vitrine site should stay light to edit.
parentsdouceur.result: Site shipped. For me, a solo project end to end (UI/UX and dev) in direct contact with the client, a useful exercise in keeping art direction and code aligned with no middleman.
parentsdouceur.seoDescription: Custom WordPress showcase site for an independent perinatal practitioner: UI/UX, development and launch by Emeric Guyon, freelance web developer.

inria.seoTitle: MALT Inria — memory profiling in Vue.js · Emeric Guyon
inria.description: Memory profiling tool to track malloc allocations.
inria.longDescription: Full rewrite of MALT, an open-source memory profiling tool developed by INRIA to track malloc/free allocations in C/C++ programs. I migrated the interface from Angular to Vue 3 + TypeScript, with a lot of work on the D3 visualizations.
inria.approach: The brief was to move a scientific tool from Angular to Vue + TypeScript without degrading the experience of the researchers who use it daily. Once the base was stable and the plugins refreshed, I reworked the readability of the graphs and added the interactions that were missing.
inria.takeaway1: Full migration from Angular to Vue 3 + TypeScript, plugins updated, existing behavior preserved 1:1 to avoid breaking users' habits.
inria.takeaway2: Source code visualizer rebuilt from scratch: per-file navigation, annotated lines, detailed popups on memory allocations per line and per function.
inria.takeaway3: D3 graphs reworked for legibility, design and interactions, plus TanStack Query to cache calls, essential once profiling datasets climb to several MB.
inria.stackNote: Vue.js + TypeScript was required by INRIA, and it's a strong fit for a tool that spends its time rendering data: typing cuts down on silent errors. D3.js stayed from V1, which makes sense for highly custom visualizations like an annotated code viewer. I added TanStack Query for caching: on this kind of dataset, you never want to fire the same request twice.
inria.result: Live on the official memtt/malt repo, open-source, used by the C/C++ community doing memory profiling. The maintainers' feedback was that the interface and source code are clearer and more readable than V1. On a personal level, this is the project that forced me to dig deep into D3 on genuinely complex visualizations, territory you rarely run into on standard web projects.
inria.seoDescription: MALT, an open-source C/C++ memory profiling tool for INRIA (Grenoble): Angular to Vue 3 migration and D3 visualizations. A freelance mission by Emeric Guyon.

uplexa.seoTitle: uPlexa — crypto site rebuild in Next.js · Emeric Guyon
uplexa.description: Volunteer rebuild of uPlexa's official site: privacy crypto plus IoT mining.
uplexa.longDescription: Rebuild of uPlexa's official website, for a privacy-focused cryptocurrency mined via IoT devices. A solo volunteer project after I joined the community as a dev and user: the old site was dated and the team wanted something more professional and cleaner.
uplexa.approach: A crypto vitrine site has two jobs: explain the project (privacy, IoT mining) to a tech audience, and build trust. I did a full Next.js rebuild with i18n for an international community, covering the classic sections of a serious crypto project: presentation, IoT mining, roadmap, team, wallet and exchange.
uplexa.takeaway1: Full Next.js rebuild, moving from a basic vitrine to a more professional, cleaner site that holds up for a serious crypto project.
uplexa.takeaway2: Native Next.js i18n to reach uPlexa's international community.
uplexa.takeaway3: Volunteer contribution: the brief here was just the wish to do better for something I believed in, no client spec attached.
uplexa.stackNote: Next.js without Tailwind, more traditional CSS to keep the vitrine light. Next-side i18n for the multilingual layer. A deliberately simple stack: for a volunteer community site, the priority is that another dev can pick it up without friction.
uplexa.result: Still live on uplexa.com. On a personal level, a community contribution project.
uplexa.seoDescription: Rebuild of the official uPlexa cryptocurrency website in Next.js: design, performance and integration, delivered pro bono by Emeric Guyon, freelance developer.
